items.summary: The Delhi High Court recently held that stamp duty on an arbitral award must be calculated on the principal amount awarded and not on the interest component even where such interest forms part of the total sum awarded by an arbitral tribunal. [ Patel KNR Infrastructure Ltd v. NHAI ] Justice Jasmeet Singh held that Section 23 of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 makes it clear that the mere inclusion of an interest component in an instrument cannot result in an enhanced stamp duty liability. "The interest component cannot be included in the computation of stamp duty merely because it forms part of the total amount awarded by the Arbitral Tribunal," the Court observed. Justice Jasmeet Singh The Court delivered the ruling while dismissing a review petition filed by the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) against an April 2024 order directing it to pay the balance interest due to Patel KNR Infrastructure Limited under an arbitral award. NHAI argued that the arbitral award of ₹18.34 crore was insufficiently stamped because stamp duty had been calculated only on the principal amount of ₹11.75 crore, excluding approximately ₹6.49 crore awarded as interest. It contended that the deficiency rendered the award unenforceable. Patel KNR, however, relied on Section 23 of the Stamp Act to argue that interest could not be included in the stamp-duty calculation. The Court accepted this submission. "In this regard, Section 23 of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 is relevant. The provision specifically stipulates that where interest is expressly made payable by the terms of an instrument, such instrument shall not be chargeable with duty higher than that with which it would have been chargeable had no mention of interest been made therein." It further reiterated that review proceedings cannot be used to reopen issues already considered. "A review cannot be treated as an appeal in disguise or an opportunity to re-agitate issues which have already been considered," the Court said. Finding no error apparent in its April 2024 order, the Court dismissed NHAI's review petition. items.title: Karnataka High Court quashes case against snake rescuer accused of capturing King Cobra
items.summary: The Karnataka High Court recently quashed a criminal case against a snake rescuer accused of capturing and photographing a King Cobra. Justice Anant Ramanath Hegde on November 2 quashed the proceedings initiated against snake rescuer Dr. P Gowri Shankar. The Court held that the allegations did not establish that the petitioner had kept the snake in captivity, killed or injured it or uploaded its photographs on social media. “It is not the allegation that the petitioner has kept the king cobra in captivity, killed or injured [it], or uploaded the photograph,” the Court observed. Justice Anant Ramanath Hegde The case against Shankar was that he had captured a King Cobra and had taken its photograph while in captivity and also allowed others to take its photographs. The complaint against the petitioner was filed based on the social media publication where the petitioner was found in a video uploaded by a third person. The petitioner sought to quash trial court proceedings after he was booked for various offences under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. The petitioner contended that the charge sheet materials did not establish that he had hunted or captured the King Cobra. He also argued that the photographs relied upon by the State showed the snake in an open forest area and not in captivity. The State argued that the charge sheet materials indicated that the petitioner had permitted others to photograph the King Cobra and had caused the photographs and videos to be uploaded on social media. The High Court noted that the State had failed to substantiate that the King Cobra had actually been captured by the petitioner. “What is seen from the photographs produced along with the charge sheet is that the king cobra was found in the forest in an open space and it was not kept in captivity,” the Court said. The Court noted that the photographs were published on social media and not recovered from the petitioner. It also observed that he had repeatedly reported rescued King Cobras to forest officials. “That being the position, the Court cannot take a view that the petitioner has committed any of the offences as alleged in the complaint,” it held. Hence, the Court proceeded to quash the case. Advocate Akshay Swamy appeared for the petitioner. Additional State Public Prosecutor MV Anoop Kumar appeared for the State. [Read Judgment]

"No doubt, it is true, as often said, that in a contract, parties legislate for themselves, but that principle cannot imaginably be carried to the extent, where the terms of the contract are actually imbued with legislative force empowering parties to enforce terms, deciding for themselves and executing it too, as if they were judicial or quasi-judicial fora, deciding a lis and then executing the decision," the Court said. Justice JJ Munir and Justice Indrajeet Shukla In the judgment passed on October 26, the Bench added that while the Supreme Court has protected the finance companies from criminal prosecutions for taking away vehicles in such cases, they are not allowed to use force merely because a clause in the agreement authorizes them to seize the vehicle from the borrower. It cannot be done by force employing goons, styled as agents," the Court emphasised. The vehicle could not be taken into possession by employment of recovery agents, who would waylay the hirer or his driver and seize it at gunpoint, the Bench further said. items.title: The ‘right to nominate’ under DPDP: A statutory right with no statutory procedure
items.summary: As more of a person’s life moves online, a need has emerged to address what happens when an individual dies or is unable to access their digital data due to incapacity. India’s new data protection law attempts to address this through the nomination right but leaves gaps that a data fiduciary must fill to comply with the legislation's objectives. Section 14(1) of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (“ DP Act ”) allows an individual, the data principal, to nominate any other person who may, on the data principal’s death or incapacity, exercise that individual’s statutory rights under the DP Act and the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 (“ DP Rules ”). The Act grants the nominee broad authority to exercise powers as if stepping into the shoes of the data principal. Does the right to nominate fill the gap it was designed to fill? The gap the provision attempts to fill is genuine, but the machinery to operate it is thin. Further, because the law on whether digital personal data can be considered “property” capable of succession is still undeveloped, it can lead to conflict when an heir stakes a competing claim. Section 38, which provides that the DP Act prevails in the event of conflict with other laws, does not address the question related to succession or access rights of the heirs. Thus, this creates considerable ambiguity for all stakeholders. As the law stands, without legislative guidance, conflicts may arise between nominees and an individual's legal heirs. The Supreme Court confirmed in its December 2023 judgment in Shakti Yezdani v. Jayanand Jayant Salgaonkar that nomination under Indian law creates neither a statutory testament nor a third line of succession. A situation could arise where a nominee wishes to delete the data, but the heirs require retention for probate, tax, or litigation. items.title: Why Ambedkar rejected ritualistic Buddhism and embraced rationality | Y S Alone on Seeking Sangha #3 | WYI
items.summary: How did B R Ambedkar reinterpret Buddhism, and why did he see it as a path towards a more equal society? What did he challenge in traditional Buddhist practices, and how does his vision of Buddhism go beyond individual spirituality to questions of social justice, rationality and collective liberation? Listen & follow on Youtube Listen & follow on Apple Listen & follow on Spotify In the third episode of Seeking Sangha, a special focus series on What’s Your ISM?, The News Minute Executive Editor Sudipto Mondal speaks to scholar YS Alone about Ambedkar’s radical interpretation of Buddhism. They discuss how Ambedkar challenged dominant readings of Buddhist philosophy, questioned ritualistic practices and drew on the Buddha’s emphasis on knowledge and rationality to formulate an alternative to caste hierarchy. They also explore Alone’s concept of “protected ignorance” and how knowledge production can be used to conceal ignorance and preserve social hierarchies. From Ambedkar’s vision of Prabuddha Bharat (Enlightened India) to the role of the Buddhist Sangha, the conversation examines why Buddhism, for Ambedkar, was not merely a path to personal peace but a philosophy rooted in social transformation, equality and justice. items.summary: Early Buddhism challenged existing social hierarchies, but how far did its ideas of equality extend? What do the Buddha’s views on women and the rules of the Sangha reveal about the contradictions within the tradition? Drawing on her work, including The Social Dimensions of Early Buddhism, they discuss the Buddha’s vision of an egalitarian society, the relationship between Buddhism and Brahmanism, and the role of the Sangha in challenging existing social hierarchies. They also explore how Buddhist ideas of compassion and liberation influenced anti-caste thought, why B R Ambedkar turned to Buddhism, and how his interpretation of early Buddhism offered an alternative to caste hierarchy. items.title: Meat-eaters a security threat? Bengaluru’s Anekal meat shops shut ahead of Modi’s visit
items.summary: Meat shops in parts of Bengaluru’s Anekal taluk will remain shut for over a day ahead of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s visit to the area on November 13, with the district administration invoking prohibitory powers under the BNSS citing security concerns. The order, issued on November 10 by Bengaluru Urban Deputy Commissioner and District Magistrate P S Kantharaju, prohibits the sale of meat within the limits of Jigani Town Municipal Council (TMC) and Kallubalu Gram Panchayat in Anekal taluk. The restriction came into effect at 6 am on Thursday, November 12, and will remain in force until 4 pm on Friday, November 13. The administration invoked Section 163(1) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023, following a request from the Bengaluru Rural District Superintendent of Police Chandrakanth MV. The police cited security arrangements for Modi and other Central and state dignitaries attending the Golden Jubilee celebrations of Prashanti Kutiram in Anekal. The event is being organised by the Swami Vivekananda Yoga Anusandhana Samsthana (S-VYASA). The police said “there was a possibility of anti-social elements or miscreants disrupting law and order” during the Prime Minister's visit. The administration said the restriction was a precautionary measure to maintain public peace during the event. The order has drawn criticism from the CPI(ML) Liberation, which condemned the temporary ban on meat and liquor sales, calling it an assault on constitutional rights. In a statement, the party said the order infringed on people's rights to personal liberty, freedom of religion and conscience, and the freedom to choose their food and livelihood. The party also criticised the Congress government in Karnataka, questioning why such an order had been issued under a government that claims to uphold constitutional freedoms and oppose the Sangh Parivar. CPI(ML) Liberation alleged that the restriction was an extension of what it described as attempts to impose a Brahminical dietary code on religious minorities, Dalits and Adivasis. It demanded the immediate withdrawal of the order. Meanwhile, Modi on Friday, November 13, inaugurated the 7.5-km elevated section of the Namma Metro Pink Line, built at a cost of around Rs 3,470 crore. He and Karnataka Chief Minister DK Shivakumar were present at the inauguration.
